A.explanation: Area under a $v$-$t$ graph is displacement, so the triangle under PQ equals the distance fallen from release to first impact, which is the initial height.

B.explanation: The rebound speed magnitude at R is smaller than the impact speed at Q and later peaks get smaller, so kinetic energy is lost and the bounces are inelastic.

C.explanation: Gradient of a $v$-$t$ graph is acceleration, and RS is free flight between bounces, so its gradient equals the acceleration of free fall.

D.explanation: Upwards velocity is the negative direction here, so maximum upwards speed is the most negative value at R just after the bounce, not the near-zero value at P.

hints: Notice the sign on the graph: the first fall OQ goes positive, so positive $v$ means downwards and negative $v$ means upwards.
Recall that area under $v$-$t$ is displacement and gradient of $v$-$t$ is acceleration, and check what PQ and RS represent in the motion.
Compare the $v$ values at P near the $t$-axis with the large negative $v$ just after the first bounce to see where the largest upwards speed occurs.
walkthrough: Take downwards as positive because the released ball gains positive $v$ along OQ to point Q just before first impact.
For the first fall, displacement = area under $v$-$t$, so the triangular area under PQ is the distance dropped, which is the initial height above the ground.

At Q the velocity jumps almost vertically to R, from large positive to large negative. The magnitude after is smaller and successive S peaks are lower, showing speed and kinetic energy are lost, so collisions are inelastic.
Between bounces the ball is in free fall, so the straight line RS must have gradient $a = \Delta v / \Delta t$ equal to the acceleration due to free fall.

Maximum upwards velocity means maximum speed in the negative direction. Point P is where the line crosses $v = 0$, while point R is the most negative $v$ just after rebound. Hence the statement about P is not correct. This is option D
